name: concept-map
title: Concept map
tagline: Concept map — concept boxes joined by labelled directed links (the relationship on each arrow); auto-laid-out free graph, any node or link label occludable.
description: A concept map: concept boxes joined by directed arrows, each arrow carrying the relationship between the two concepts ("the Sun — provides energy for → plants — eaten by → herbivores"). Unlike the rest of the diagram family it is a free, many-to-many directed graph — one concept can have several incoming and outgoing links, and a cross-link can close a cycle. You author only the graph (the concepts as nodes, and the links as from/to pairs each with a relationship label); the model derives every box's size from its wrapped label, every box position from a layered auto-layout, every arrow's route — including cross-links and cycles that curve around a side margin — and the placement of each relationship label on the middle of its own arrow (with a background halo so it reads over the line). Any concept can be occluded to "?" ("which concept goes here?"), and — the signature question — any relationship label can be occluded to ask "what is the relationship between these two?". Concepts and links highlight in amber to mark an answer or trace a path. For a single central idea with one ring of unlabelled branches use diagram/mind-map; for a single-parent hierarchy use diagram/tree; for an algorithm with decision diamonds and loops use diagram/flowchart.
whenToUse: Reach for this to draw a concept map: several concepts joined by directed arrows, each arrow labelled with the relationship between the two concepts, so the figure reads as a web of sentences ("photosynthesis — produces → glucose"). It is the model for showing how ideas relate with named relationships — synoptic links in science (energy flow, the carbon/water cycle, body systems), systems and cause-webs in geography (causes and effects of climate change, a river system), and "link these concepts" revision tasks across subjects. Author the graph: list the concepts as `nodes` (each an id + a noun-phrase label) and the relationships as `links` (each `from` one concept id `to` another, with the relationship as its `label` — write it as the verb phrase that makes "from label to" a sentence). The layout, box sizes, arrow routes and label placement are all derived, so you never position anything. A concept may have many incoming and outgoing links, and a link may point back at an earlier concept to close a cycle (it routes around a side margin). Conventions: keep relationship labels short verb phrases; keep roughly three to six links leaving any one rank so the map stays readable (a genuinely all-to-all tangle is out of scope in v1 — split it into two maps); keep `direction` consistent across a lesson ("down", the default, reads top-to-bottom; "right" suits a left-to-right cause-chain). Nodes are a neutral grey by default so the relationships carry the eye — set a node `color` only to mark out genuinely distinct categories of concept (inputs vs outputs, causes vs effects). Questions: occlude a link label to ask "what is the relationship?" (the defining concept-map question), or occlude a node to ask "which concept goes here?" — the rest of the map stays visible; highlight a concept or link to mark the answer. Staged build: keep the concepts fixed and reveal links / move the highlight along a synoptic path stage by stage (the layout never moves). Synonyms a teacher might use: concept map, knowledge map, relationship map, semantic map, linking words, synoptic links, cause and effect web, systems diagram, "link these ideas". Switch model when the picture changes: a single central idea ringed by one level of unlabelled branches (no links between them) is diagram/mind-map; a strict single-parent classification / family hierarchy is diagram/tree; an algorithm or procedure with decision diamonds and control-flow loops is diagram/flowchart.

id.description: Unique kebab-case id for this concept, referenced by links (e.g. "sun", "photosynthesis", "carbon-dioxide"). Not shown to pupils — it is the wiring handle.

label.description: The concept written inside the box, wrapped to fit (e.g. "Photosynthesis", "Carbon dioxide"). Keep it to a noun / noun phrase — the relationship goes on the link, not in the box.

occlude.description: Render this concept's label as "?" — the "which concept goes here?" hook. The box and all links stay drawn and the hidden word never leaks into the aria description. Default false.

highlight.description: Amber this concept — the answer, or the box reached when a staged build traces a path through the map. Default false.

color.description: Override THIS concept's colour. Nodes default to a neutral grey so the relationships carry the eye; set a colour ONLY to mark out genuinely distinct CATEGORIES of concept (e.g. inputs vs outputs, causes vs effects) — colour every node in a category the same. A reserved role keyword (accent, accent-2…accent-5, ink, muted, scaffold) keeps it brand-themeable; a colour literal (#hex, rgb()/rgba(), hsl()/hsla(), or a CSS named colour like "teal") is honoured exactly and opts this box OUT of brand reskinning. Ignored on a highlighted box (amber is reserved).

nodes.description: The concepts of the map. Each has a unique id and a label. Order does not matter — positions are derived from the links.

from.description: Id of the concept the arrow leaves (the relationship reads from here).

to.description: Id of the concept the arrow enters. A link whose target sits at or above its source — a cross-link that closes a cycle — is routed around a side margin automatically, so a cycle (e.g. "respiration returns CO₂") draws cleanly.

label.description: The RELATIONSHIP / linking phrase on this arrow — the heart of a concept map ("provides energy for", "is eaten by", "produces", "causes", "is a type of"). Written as the verb phrase that makes "FROM — label → TO" read as a sentence. Drawn at the middle of the arrow with a background halo so it reads over the line; wrapped if long. Omit only for a bare association.

occlude.description: Render this link's relationship label as "?" — the signature concept-map question, "what is the relationship between these two concepts?". The arrow and both concepts stay drawn; the hidden phrase never leaks into the aria. Default false.

highlight.description: Amber this link and its label — the answer relationship, or the active link when a staged build traces a path. Default false.

color.description: Override THIS link's colour (and its relationship label) — so one relationship can be picked out without recolouring the rest. Wins over the figure-wide `colors.links`. A reserved role keyword (accent, accent-2…accent-5, ink, muted, scaffold) stays brand-themeable; a colour literal (#hex, rgb()/rgba(), hsl()/hsla(), or a CSS named colour) is honoured exactly and opts this link OUT of brand reskinning. Ignored on a highlighted link (amber is reserved).

links.description: The directed, labelled arrows: each runs from one node id to another and carries the relationship between them as its `label`. The same concept can be the `to` of several links and the `from` of several others; point a link back at an earlier concept to close a cycle.

direction.description: Reading flow: "down" (default) lays the map top-to-bottom; "right" lays a left-to-right cause-chain. Keep it consistent across a lesson.

header.description: Optional short title centred above the figure; the top padding grows to clear it.

caption.description: Optional line centred below the figure, e.g. a short context note. Never the question or an instruction: that wording is the block's text.

colors.description: Optional figure-wide colour overrides — set ONLY when an author/teacher explicitly asks ("make the links grey"). Omit to keep the themeable defaults. A per-link `color` overrides this for one arrow; a per-node `color` overrides a concept's colour.

links.description: Default colour of every arrow and its relationship label, replacing the near-black ink. A reserved role keyword (accent, accent-2…accent-5, ink, muted, scaffold) stays brand-themeable; a colour literal (#hex, rgb()/rgba(), hsl()/hsla(), or a CSS named colour like "teal") is honoured exactly. A single arrow can still differ via its own `color`.

examples.label: Worked example — photosynthesis (two reactants and the Sun feed one process, which produces two outputs)
Answer space — every relationship label hidden ("write the relationship on each arrow")
Occluded question — one concept hidden ("which group completes the energy flow?")
Hard case — the carbon cycle: a dense web where respiration closes three cycles back to CO₂
Left-to-right map — water flowing to the sea, with a split and a merge (direction: right)
Author-set colours — reactants / process / products colour-coded, the answer link highlighted
